stories.title: Jake's Lake
stories.story:
**The Lake That Ice Made**

Jake's boots made soft sounds on the dock. Mist danced over the lake like smoke. The water was so still, it looked fake—like a huge mirror someone dropped in the forest.

"I will make the biggest wave!" Jake said to himself.

He wanted to wake up the whole lake. Make it remember it was not just a mirror.

Jake picked up a smooth stone. Cold in his hand. He threw it hard and—

*SPLASH!*

Just tiny waves. That was it? 

He tried again. Bigger stone. 

*Plunk!*

Still just small waves that died fast.

Jake's face went red. The lake was too big. Too deep. He was too small.

Then something white caught his eye. There, by the cave—huge scratches in the rock. Like giant claws had scraped the stone.

"Whoa," Jake said.

He ran to the cave. The grooves were deep as his whole hand. Smooth as glass.

"Ice made those," came a voice.

Jake spun around. An old woman stood there, her hair white as mist.

"Ice?" Jake asked.

"Ice thick as ten homes. Heavy as a mountain. It came down this valley like a river. Scraped and carved. Dug this whole lake with its huge weight."

Jake stared at the scratches. Then at the water.

"The ice made the lake?"

The woman gave a smile. "Made it deep. Made it wide. Then it melted and gave the valley this gift."

Jake looked out at the water again. It didn't seem too big now. It seemed... perfect. Made by something even bigger than him. Something that was brave enough to carve a home for itself, then brave enough to let go.

He picked up one more stone. Not to wake the lake this time. 

Just to say hello.

The waves spread out in circles, each one carrying the morning light like a message across the water that ancient ice had made.

stories.title: Bake Day
stories.story:
**Morning Magic**

Wake, wake, wake—
Grandma's hands take
white dust from the cave
of her cupboard.

Same as always,
same as always—
the wooden spoon scrapes
the blue bowl's curve.

Heat waits brave
behind the oven door.
Sweet crystals gave
their fine names
to butter's game
of melting, melting.

Crack. Crack.
Eggs break their shells,
make yellow suns
swim in white clouds.

Wire whisk sings its tune.
Bubbles rise like tiny moons.
The mix takes its name
from nothing but
this dance of dust and flame.

Tick. Tick.
The timer's tame beat
counts the cave-dark oven's
secret work.

What was wet
becomes cake.
What was cold
grows brave with warmth.
What was just white dust
wakes up golden,
tall and wide.

Steam escapes
the oven's mouth—
sweet breath
of transformation,
warm on my face
like summer rain
from an inside lake.

Grandma's smile
holds the same magic
as her mixing bowl:
everything plain
can wake up
quite fine.

stories.title: Mike's Bike Ride
stories.story:
**The Wobble**

Jake rode his bike on the pine path. The trees made shade above his head.

"Just like we did at home," Mom said. "Let go when you feel brave."

His hands felt wet on the bike. Pine cones lay on the path. A bird made noise up in the trees.

Jake began to ride. The bike went slow at first.

Mom's hand left his back.

The front wheel began to shake left and right. Jake felt scared. The bike wanted to go this way and that way. He held on tight.

Bad choice.

The shake got big. Left. Right. Left more.

Jake's hands went white. The bike went close to the pine trees.

Then he thought what Dad said: *Don't fight the wobble. Ride with it.*

Jake let his hands be loose. The wheel found its own way. The bike went straight, like magic. The fast he went, the more it stayed straight.

Wind went past his face. Sunshine came through the pine trees and danced on his arms. The path got wide ahead.

Mom's voice got small behind him: "You did it! You did it!"

Jake went around a curve. The bike felt like part of him. Pine smell filled his nose. His shade raced next to him on the path, boy and bike as one in the warm day.

stories.title: A Home for Mole
stories.story:
**The Name Game**

Jake the mole woke in his cave. His nose felt something new.

The tunnel walls felt wrong—too wide. The air had a strange smell.

Jake had been digging for days, following the sweet smell of cake from the house above. But where was he now?

His whiskers brushed against cold stone. The tunnel maze he knew was gone.

"Hello?" Jake called. His voice came back hollow.

He put his nose to the ground. There—a faint trace of his path. But which way? Left smelled like wet leaves. Right smelled like... nothing.

Jake's heart beat fast.

Then he thought of what his mother used to say: "When you can't see your way, make a new game."

Jake began to hum his own name. "Jake, Jake, Jake." He tapped it out with his paws—one beat for each sound. Then he listened.

The sound bounced left and died fast. It bounced right and sang back long and clear.

Jake smiled in the dark. The tunnel to the right was longer, deeper—just like the one that led home.

He followed his name-song through the earth, tapping and humming, until warm air touched his whiskers and the sweet smell of home filled his nose.

Jake curled up in his own soft cave, still humming his tune.
